Looking at this problem, I need to determine the maximum number of alternating streets out of 10 lines in general position.

**Answer: 10 — all streets can be made alternating simultaneously.**

## Proof

**Setup.** The main/side assignment at each intersection is equivalent to orienting $K_{10}$: for each pair $\{i,j\}$, either $i$ is main over $j$ or vice versa. For line $i$, let $r_i(j)$ denote the position (1-indexed) of the intersection with line $j$ in the order along line $i$. Since line $i$ has 9 intersections, reversing the travel direction sends $r_i(j) \mapsto 10 - r_i(j)$, which has the **same parity** (as 10 is even). So $\text{parity}(r_i(j))$ is well-defined.

**Alternating condition.** Line $i$ is alternating iff its main/side status alternates along its 9 intersections, meaning $i$ is main at positions of one parity and side at the other. So there exists $p_i \in \{0,1\}$ such that:
$$i \text{ is main over } j \iff \text{parity}(r_i(j)) = p_i.$$

**Consistency constraint.** For lines $i$ and $j$ to both be alternating, we need $i$ main over $j$ iff $j$ is side to $i$:
$$\text{parity}(r_i(j)) = p_i \iff \text{parity}(r_j(i)) \neq p_j,$$
which gives $p_i \oplus p_j = 1 \oplus s_{ij}$, where $s_{ij} := \text{parity}(r_i(j)) \oplus \text{parity}(r_j(i))$.

**Global consistency.** All 10 lines are alternating iff the system $p_i \oplus p_j = 1 \oplus s_{ij}$ is solvable over $\mathbb{F}_2$. This holds iff every triangle $\{i,j,k\}$ satisfies:
$$s_{ij} \oplus s_{jk} \oplus s_{ki} = 1. \quad (\star)$$

**Key lemma: $(\star)$ always holds.** Consider three lines $i, j, k$ forming triangle $T$ with vertices $P_{ij}, P_{jk}, P_{ki}$. Let:
- $a$ = number of other lines crossing the edge of $T$ on line $i$ (segment $P_{ij}P_{ik}$),
- $b$ = number crossing the edge on line $j$,
- $c$ = number crossing the edge on line $k$.

Each of the 7 remaining lines is a straight line not through any vertex of $T$ (by general position). Since $T$ is convex, each such line crosses $T$ either **0 or 2 times**, contributing 0 or 2 to $a+b+c$. Therefore:
$$a + b + c \text{ is even.}$$

Now compute $s_{ij} \oplus s_{jk} \oplus s_{ki}$. On line $i$, the 7 other intersections (besides $P_{ij}, P_{ik}$) split as: $\alpha$ on the ray from $P_{ij}$ away from $P_{ik}$, $a$ on segment $P_{ij}P_{ik}$, $\beta$ on the ray from $P_{ik}$ away from $P_{ij}$, with $\alpha + a + \beta = 7$. Then:
$$\text{parity}(r_i(j)) \oplus \text{parity}(r_i(k)) = (1+\alpha) \oplus (1+\beta) = \alpha + \beta = 7 - a \equiv 1 + a \pmod{2}.$$

By the same argument on lines $j$ and $k$:
$$\text{parity}(r_j(i)) \oplus \text{parity}(r_j(k)) \equiv 1 + b, \quad \text{parity}(r_k(i)) \oplus \text{parity}(r_k(j)) \equiv 1 + c \pmod{2}.$$

Combining:
$$s_{ij} \oplus s_{jk} \oplus s_{ki} = (1+a) + (1+b) + (1+c) \equiv 3 + (a+b+c) \equiv 1 + 0 = 1 \pmod{2}. \quad \checkmark$$

**Conclusion.** Since $(\star)$ holds for every triangle and every line arrangement, the system $p_i \oplus p_j = 1 \oplus s_{ij}$ is always consistent. The solution determines a valid tournament (the consistency condition ensures each edge is oriented exactly one way), and with this assignment, **all 10 lines are alternating**.

The maximum possible number of alternating streets is $\boxed{10}$.
